comparison: Both evaluations support the core findings from Experiments 1-2 showing listeners can segregate foreground tone sequences from complex backgrounds. OpenEval focuses on C2, C19-C22 (parametric effects and rapid learning), while peer review covers a broader set (C2-C3, C19-C25) including the AXB discrimination task. Both affirm the experimental controls and basic segregation findings.

OpenEval evaluates the AXB discrimination task (C24-C25, C43) as strongly supporting object-level representation. Peer review includes C24-C25 in their broader affirmation of segregation findings. Both support these claims, though OpenEval provides more detailed reasoning about ruling out low-level confounds.

OpenEval supports the power control methodology (C23, C73-C74) as eliminating confounds. Peer review includes C23 in their broader affirmation that 'studies were appropriately performed with adequate controls.' Both agree on the adequacy of experimental controls.

Perfect claim overlap (C32, C33, C44) but divergent evaluations. OpenEval finds the statistical evidence clearly supports discrete temporal unit processing. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, requesting clearer motivation and model predictions for this manipulation, suggesting incomplete theoretical grounding despite the behavioral finding.

Perfect claim overlap (C34, C35, C45) but divergent evaluations. OpenEval finds the graded performance degradation with frequency ramps clearly supports dynamic frequency tracking. Peer reviewers find the interpretation incomplete without model predictions, specifically requesting 'what the model predicts for the ramped SFG.'

Perfect claim overlap (C36, C37) but divergent evaluations. OpenEval finds the null effect of background presence strongly supports rejection of adaptation mechanisms. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about the mechanistic interpretation, requesting model predictions to support the conclusion.

Both evaluations support the noise interruption findings (C38, C46). OpenEval emphasizes the robustness demonstrated by the null effect. Peer reviewers explicitly highlight this as 'remarkable,' affirming the finding without critique. Strong agreement on this experimental result.

Overlapping claims (C39, C40, C47) about long temporal integration windows. Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval also addresses C41-C42 about cortical involvement. Peer review emphasizes the remarkable nature of 500ms integration, with both affirming the robustness of the findings.

Both evaluations support the inference about cortical involvement (C41, C42). OpenEval finds the inference reasonable given known A1 temporal windows. Peer reviewers explicitly agree, stating findings are 'clearly beyond the segregation capacities of core auditory cortex' and authors 'rightfully suggest non-classical auditory cortical processing stations.'

Perfect claim overlap (C5, C26, C27, C28) regarding inadequacy of adaptation-based models. Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval emphasizes the logical arguments from stimulus properties. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this by affirming the need for alternative models and endorsing temporal coherence as most appropriate.

High claim overlap (C6, C7, C29, C48, C55) regarding temporal coherence model support. OpenEval finds qualitative correspondence sufficient for support with appropriate qualifications. Peer reviewers express disappointment with 'integration between data and modeling' and note model simulations aren't shown for all manipulations, creating uncertainty despite acknowledging the model as 'most appropriate.'

Both evaluations express uncertainty about the novelty claim (C49). OpenEval notes it requires comprehensive literature knowledge for verification. Peer reviewers' uncertainty about model completeness indirectly affects confidence in novelty claims. Both find the claim unverifiable from available evidence.

Perfect claim overlap (C62-C65, C70-C71) regarding IPS involvement but divergent evaluations. OpenEval finds these claims speculative, requiring direct experimental validation beyond the cited fMRI study. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse the interpretation, stating authors 'rightfully suggest non-classical auditory cortical processing stations,' showing greater confidence in the IPS hypothesis.

OpenEval evaluates claims about current knowledge gaps and animal studies (C58-C61) as appropriately qualified statements. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these literature review claims.

OpenEval evaluates background/motivation claims (C1, C8-C10, C14, C16) as well-supported by citations and accurate field characterizations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory claims.

OpenEval evaluates literature summary claims (C11-C13, C15, C17-C18) as accurate characterizations with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background literature claims.

OpenEval evaluates theoretical framework descriptions (C30-C31, C50-C54) as accurate with proper attribution to prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these theoretical background claims.

OpenEval finds claims about salience representation and neural implementation (C56-C57) speculative, requiring direct neurophysiological validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific mechanistic inferences.

OpenEval evaluates parietal anatomy and function claims (C66-C69) as well-supported by appropriate citations to established knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these anatomical background claims.

OpenEval evaluates methodological claims (C72-C76) as appropriate and meeting standard experimental requirements. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological details.
